blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Bounding In-Flight Work**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Multi-Agent Coordination, § Bounding In-Flight Work
blocks.md: Suppose the supervisor cancels `migration_task_01` while `worker_interface_01` awaits an external test job and `worker_caller_01` finishes generating a candidate patch. Even if the caller's patch passes its local validation checks after the supervisor initiates cancellation, the runtime must ensure that the patch remains strictly unpublishable. Meanwhile, an external testing service may have already accepted the interface worker's test request, incurring resource and billing charges that remain unsettled long after the worker process halts. In single-agent execution, a cancellation signal interrupts a local loop or an outstanding remote inference call.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Cancellation context trees
- Evidence preservation during cleanup
- Hedged requests and speculative work
- Credit-based flow control

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Subtree cancellation matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Cancellation scope follows delegation lineage and closes admission at each gate, but cancelling a subtree does not settle the obligations its admitted work already created.

questions.q: The section **Bounding In-Flight Work** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Cancellation scope follows delegation lineage and closes admission at each gate, but cancelling a subtree does not settle the obligations its admitted work already created.
The runtime assigns each child an identity and a grant contained in its delegator's, sharing permissions but partitioning consumable allowances by atomic reservation.
Under Speedup(N) = 1/((1-p) + p/N + c(N)) any gain requires c(N) < p(1 - 1/N), the best count sits near sqrt(p/c) for linear overhead, and the serial fraction caps speedup at 1/(1-p).

For a fixed amount of work with no coordination overhead, the serial fraction 1-p caps speedup at 1/(1-p) however many workers are added, and the universal scalability law reduces to it when coherency is zero.
